ESR breaks ground on JPY120 bil large-scale logistics development in Greater Tokyo
article:
Construction has started on a sprawling 310,000 sq m (3.34 million sq ft) logistics development in Kawasaki, Greater Tokyo, scheduled for completion in 2Q2029.

Real asset owner and manager ESR on Nov 20 announced it has broken ground on the nine-storey Higashi Ogishima Distribution B (HOB), backed by a consortium of global and Japanese institutional investors.

The JPY120 billion (about $974.6 million) project will offer next-generation logistics space in “one of Japan’s most sought-after markets”, amid strong customer demand and moderating new supply, ESR said.

HOB is the second building within the ESR Higashi Ogishima Distribution Centre logistics hub — a multi-year, multibillion-dollar development that began with ESR’s acquisition of both sites in 2016 and is set to provide some 660,000 sq m of logistics space in total.

The other building is the 350,000 sq m Higashi Ogishima Distribution Centre A (HOA), completed in 2023 and over 87% occupied today.

Stuart Gibson, co-founder and co-CEO of ESR, said that HOB will take a people-first approach and feature a bold facade designed by world-renowned industrial designer Marc Newson.

Retail, relaxation, green and shared spaces, and amenities throughout the development are intended to enhance the workplace experience and support employee wellbeing.

HOB will also have a double-ramp configuration for efficient vehicle access, as well as flexible and environmentally conscious building specifications. Its resilience features will include seismic base isolation and emergency power systems.

“Our ambition is to create the finest logistics property in Japan: a building customers want, that works hard for their businesses, and that is highly profitable and accretive for our investors,” Gibson said.

ESR brought together 23 Japanese investors and a long-standing European capital partner to develop HOB.

This demonstrates continued institutional demand for high-quality logistics real estate in Greater Tokyo, the company noted.

ESR added that the investment comes amid favourable fundamentals for large multi-tenant logistics properties, with new supply expected to dwindle through 2027, alongside rising rents and declining vacancy.

title: Newly completed freehold industrial building on Kim Chuan Terrace hits market at $35 mil
article:
A newly completed freehold industrial building at 6 Kim Chuan Terrace has been put up for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise, with a guide price of $35 million.

The corner property is zoned Business 2 (B2) and sits on a site of about 8,906 sq ft in the Tai Seng–Kim Chuan industrial area. Its built-up area of about 25,794 sq ft means the guide price works out to about $1,357 psf.

The building obtained its Temporary Occupation Permit in 2025 and its Certificate of Statutory Completion in January 2026, so a buyer can fit it out and move in without waiting for construction.

The closest recent comparable is 3 Kim Chuan Lane, a freehold B2 building completed in 2014. On Nov 13, Westlite Dormitory, the workers’ accommodation arm of Centurion Corporation, agreed to buy it from Goodland Group for $61 million. That works out to about $1,463 psf on its built-up area of about 41,710 sq ft, on a 16,685 sq ft site.

On Kim Chuan Terrace itself, two freehold plots have changed hands. No. 25, at 5,883 sq ft, sold for $12.3 million in June, or about $2,091 psf of land. No. 27, at 9,806 sq ft, sold for $18.25 million in July 2025, or about $1,861 psf of land.

Steward Asia, an agency team under PropNex, is marketing 6 Kim Chuan Terrace. Alvin Tan, Steward Asia's team lead, estimates that after stamp duty, planning, financing costs, and two to three years of construction, the all-in cost of building on these two sites could exceed $1,600 psf on gross floor area.

Nearby freehold strata industrial launches have also sold quickly. All 66 units at CT Gold @ MacPherson on Lorong Bakar Batu were taken up within two days of its late April launch, at $1,500 to $1,600 psf. Generations @ Tannery on Tannery Lane sold all 59 units on its launch day in July, at $1,700 to $2,000 psf. Space Nova at 21 New Industrial Road achieved an 87% take-up of its 47 units on booking day in early August, at $1,475 to $2,161 psf.

Loyalle Chin, co-founder of Steward Asia, notes that industrial prices are up 4.2% y-o-y and that all new industrial land is now sold on 20- to 30-year leases. “A freehold building with no lease decay lets a family enterprise grow within it and pass it on to the next generation,” he says.

The property is not subject to Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty, and foreigners and companies are eligible to buy. The EOI exercise closes at 3pm on Jan 15, 2027.

title: The Assembly Place JV to run 662-bed student housing at SUTD’s new DIVE Collective
article:
A joint venture between The Assembly Place (TAP) and TS Group will finance, fit out and run the student accommodation at DIVE Collective, a new development at the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) that combines student housing with an innovation hub and workspaces for start-ups.

The development’s two 14-storey blocks will add 522 rooms with 662 beds, raising SUTD’s student housing capacity by about 60% from the current 1,000-plus beds across three hostel blocks. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong officiated the groundbreaking of DIVE Collective.

SUTD selected TS Group as its development partner through a request for proposal. TS Group and Catalist-listed TAP have since formed a joint venture company, TSTAP Commune, in which TAP holds a 20% stake. Upon completion sometime in early 2029, the development will be owned by SUTD.

DIVE Collective is designed to let students sketch, prototype, test and refine ideas in one place. At its core is an SUTD-run 687 sq m (7,395 sq ft) Innovation Hub with 3D printers, workstations and space for classes, design sprints and hackathons. Next to it is Innovation Central, a sheltered open-air area for testing robots, drones and other physical AI projects.

Its 28 work suites, open round the clock, will be used by start-ups, including those founded by SUTD students and alumni, and by SUTD’s partner companies under the university’s innovation and enterprise programmes. Industry-sponsored postgraduate students will also be able to use them for projects and research.

The development anchors SUTD’s Design·AI Innovation and Venture Exploration (DIVE) platform and is one of several projects planned for the university’s DIVE campus. Two others, DIVE Physical AI and DIVE Commons, are expected to be ready in January and May 2027, respectively. Plans are underway for a new drone and robotics enclosure and a 77,000 sq m (828,828 sq ft) campus expansion after DIVE Collective is completed.

“Student accommodation has always been one of TAP’s core strengths,” said Eugene Lim, TAP’s executive director and CEO. “Together with TS Group and SUTD, we envision DIVE Collective as a vibrant, interconnected community where students, founders and industry partners come together, exchange ideas and spark collaborations.”

TS Group co-founder and COO Tome Oh said the partnership would combine TS Group’s expertise in accommodation development and operations with TAP’s experience in managing student accommodation.

title: 3 Reliable SGX Income Stocks to Help Outpace Fixed Deposit Rates
article:
Fixed deposits can be a good income instrument if you’re seeking capital preservation and a constant yield.
However, given that most 12-month fixed deposit rates (around 1.96%) barely cover
inflation
, some investors might be on the lookout for beefier income.
That’s where SGX-listed companies, with sustainable dividends and good track records of annual payments, come in.
Here, we look at three names that stand out for their dividend reliability.
However, do note that unlike
fixed deposits
, your capital is at risk and dividends can be discretionary (you might not always receive a consistent income).
DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05)
A solid blue chip renowned for consistent dividends over the past decade, DBS offers a trailing yield of around 4.8% based on the 19 November 2026 closing price of S$67.34.
This figure is particularly attractive against the current average fixed deposit yields of around 1.96%.
With an ordinary payout ratio of around 63% (about 79% including capital return dividends), the annual dividend seems sustainable, especially given the bank’s resilient earnings.
A solid balance sheet, with a low non-performing loan (NPL) ratio and a healthy capital position, further supports the dividend.
Over the past five years, DBS’ ordinary dividend has grown 142% from S$1.09 in 2021 to S$2.64 over the trailing twelve months (TTM).
Moving forward, further dividend growth is likely to come from higher earnings from its fee-generating business segments.
Stabilisation and a pickup in its net interest margin could also help.
Do note that DBS’ trailing yield also includes the bank’s capital return dividends of S$0.15 per quarter, which are ending in 2027.
Furthermore, as strong as DBS’ banking franchise is, it’s still not immune to economic downturns which could pressure its earnings and dividends.
Venture Corporation Limited (SGX: V03)
Venture Corporation stands out for its consistent dividend, with annual payments since 1992.
Like DBS, Venture Corporation offers potential income well above what fixed deposits pay, with a yield of around 5.5%.
Venture Corporation’s dividends are supported by consistent profitability, with net profit of between S$227.0 million and S$369.6 million from FY2021 to FY2025.
Crucially, the business has no bank borrowings and net cash of S$1.1 billion as at 30 June 2026, which helps to cover any shortfall when cash flows fluctuate due to working capital requirements (stocking of inventory).
One thing to be mindful of is that the payout ratio is stretched, at around 101% of FY2025 earnings; further dividend growth has to come from an increase in earnings and cash generation.
On that, management is optimistic that strong demand across its technology domains will help to drive future revenue and profit growth.
If earnings decline, Venture Corporation would have to keep dipping into its cash reserves to maintain its dividend.
Based on the current cash dividends paid, Venture Corporation’s cash position would only cover close to five years of annual payout.
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), or CICT
Another solid income name, CICT offers a trailing yield of around 4.6%.
Like the other two names, CICT has a solid track record: its distributions have quietly risen every year since the pandemic.
Backed by a quality portfolio of properties mostly in Singapore, CICT’s distributions seem well supported, especially given the REIT’s healthy rental reversions.
Management’s ability to acquire high-quality, accretive properties, such as Paragon in July 2026, also helps to boost distributions.
The balance sheet is solid, with an aggregate leverage of 39.7% and a decent interest coverage ratio of 3.8x.
With management expecting mid-single-digit rental reversions in the coming quarters, CICT’s distributions look well supported.
The REIT trades at a price-to-book (P/B) ratio of 1.1x, in line with its five-year average.
The main risk for CICT would be higher interest rates, which would eat into its distributions.

title: Abu Dhabi’s MGX gains US$20 bil from Anthropic’s listing
article:
(Nov 20): Anthropic PBC’s history-making listing has spawned a legion of winners around the world. Among them is Abu Dhabi artificial intelligence (AI) investor MGX.

Based on Anthropic’s closing price of US$97.17, MGX’s stake carried an unrealised mark-to-market gain of roughly US$20 billion, a spokesperson told Bloomberg News. That would make the two-year-old Emirati firm one of the largest institutional investors, excluding strategic holders and founders.

MGX established its initial position in Anthropic in early 2024 and later backed multiple funding rounds, one of which it co-led. The firm didn’t disclose details on commitments, but its participation over the years had helped maintain an “attractive” blended-entry valuation, the spokesperson said.

It added to its position in the Claude chatbot maker’s initial public offering. The US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement broke SpaceX’s record, and other big beneficiaries from the deal include Spark Capital, Iconiq, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

Anthropic shares fell as much as 7.4% in premarket trading on Friday. The stock had surged as much as 39% on debut before giving back more than half those gains to close 17% higher, making the firm the world’s seventh-largest public company by market value.

Chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, MGX has rapidly assembled a portfolio spanning frontier AI models, semiconductor infrastructure and data centres. In July, it raised US$49 billion for one of the largest funds ever dedicated to AI deals, and Anthropic is now one of the major contributors to the fund’s performance.

See also: Ubisoft shares plummet after rival games seen hitting sales

MGX’s gains are striking due to their magnitude but also because Dario Amodei once sought to keep Middle Eastern capital at arm’s length.

The frontier AI lab’s chief executive officer had repeatedly raised concerns about accepting money from the region’s governments, citing the risks of giving authoritarian regimes access to advanced AI. But the firm opened its doors to Gulf capital as funding needs grew.

Other entities and some regional tycoons also stand to benefit, although MGX looks set to be among the biggest gainers.

See also: Nvidia’s future without founder-CEO Jensen Huang

Alpha Dhabi Holding, also part of Sheikh Tahnoon’s business empire, has indirect exposure to Anthropic through its commitment to an Alpha Wave Ventures fund. And Dubai billionaire Hussain Sajwani recently said he expects his investments in AI firms, including Anthropic, to generate billions of dollars in returns.

Elsewhere in the Middle East, Qatar Investment Authority, the country’s US$580 billion sovereign wealth fund, has participated in at least two of Anthropic’s recent funding rounds. Like MGX, the Qatari fund has become a significant backer of technology companies in recent years.

Anthropic’s IPO comes a few months after SpaceX’s US$75 billion offering, which also benefitted a range of Gulf investors including MGX, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal.

For MGX, the deal could vindicate its rare investing hat trick: stakes in Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI, giving it exposure to three of the world’s most closely watched AI firms. Qatar’s QIA has taken a similar approach, investing in both Anthropic and xAI.

title: Anthropic drops after IPO pop as AI slump engulfs markets
article:
(Nov 20): Anthropic PBC shares fell on their second day of trading as the unwinding of the global artificial intelligence (AI) trade overshadowed the optimism that had fuelled a rally on its record-setting debut.

The Claude chatbot maker’s shares tumbled as much as 7.4% in premarket trading as of 6.20am in New York. The stock had surged as much as 39% from its IPO price on Thursday before relinquishing more than half of the gains, ending the session up 17% and making Anthropic the world’s seventh-biggest public company by market value.

Anthropic’s slide came on a gloomy day for equities, with global stocks poised for their longest losing streak in more than three years. While the initial pop reflected massive investor appetite after a heavily oversubscribed IPO, the steep valuation — combined with fresh competitive threats — weighed on the shares on Friday as traders dumped risk across markets.

“With what appeared to be the final pillar supporting the AI rally now giving way, market sentiment is now very pessimistic,” said Gerald Gan, chief investment officer at Singapore-based Reed Capital. “While I am preparing to accumulate quality stocks at more attractive valuations, I am equally mindful of the risks of catching a falling knife.”

Anthropic PBC signage during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Thursday.

See also: Saudis strike deal with Japan to replenish depleted oil stocks

MSCI Inc’s Asia Pacific equities index fell 3.3% to its lowest since April. That helped put the MSCI All Country World Index on course for its longest losing streak since September 2023. Nasdaq 100 futures slipped 1.5%.

Anthropic’s US$107.3 billion IPO had attracted global demand for seven times the shares available for sale, with competition so fierce that more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock were left empty handed, Bloomberg reported on Thursday.

The shares closed at US$97.17 on Thursday in New York, compared with the IPO price of US$83. Anthropic ended the day with a fully diluted market value of about US$1.8 trillion.

See also: Xi, Trump, Putin agree to increase supply of global fuels

The IPO vaulted Anthropic to the status of unrivalled AI industry leader — at least for the moment — and delivered billions of dollars in returns to its backers and pushed up the combined wealth of its seven founders to US$166 billion. The raise eclipsed the record set in June by SpaceX’s IPO, which ultimately totalled US$86.25 billion including overallotment shares sold by the underwriters. Goldman Sachs Group Inc, Morgan Stanley and 20 other banks earned a record US$550 million in fees for their work on Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut followed weeks of shaky trading in US stocks, as investors grappled with worries over Nvidia Corp’s role as a major backstop of the AI ecosystem following its longtime chief’s ouster. A Democratic sweep in midterm elections promises to change the industry’s regulatory landscape and could complicate approvals for new data centres.

“You’ve seen sentiment sort of continue to worsen around AI and it has not let up today,” said Jordan Watson, managing director of investments at Tandem Investment Advisors. “What’s important for markets now is Anthropic is the most transparent real-time signal of the AI risk trade.”

In a blow to sentiment, Apple Inc is developing its own autonomous AI agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta Platforms Inc and others.

Thursday’s broader market weakness was “just a continuation of what we’ve seen for the last several weeks, and that is a lot of nervousness around the semiconductor space,” said Gina Martin Adams, chief market strategist at HB Wealth. “The financing of the AI ecosystem is certainly a question that investors are asking and it’s weighing on the market at large.”

Some of the broader selloff may have also been fuelled by investors selling positions in other companies to buy Anthropic shares, she added.

The company won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers and explosive growth, with its run-rate revenue — a measure annualised from a shorter period — soaring to US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings show.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Claude Code, the company’s coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by NASA engineers, a filing shows. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering US$100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.

“We are impressed by the wealth creation this company is generating, in a matter of a few years and with reasonable free cash flow burn,” said Raphael Thuin, head of capital markets strategies at Tikehau Capital. “To get exposed to AI though, we tend to favour more diversified businesses, and in any case we would like to see the post IPO volatility fade before engaging further.”

A major challenge will be taming ballooning costs for AI infrastructure and reliably delivering operational profitability. Anthropic reported a US$567 million operating loss in the third quarter, primarily driven by US$5 billion of computing costs under short-term commitments and US$2 billion of non-cash charges related to the company’s charitable donation-matching programme.

Goldman Sachs research analysts expect the company to take until 2030 to generate positive free cash flow on an annual basis. That said, they are modelling Anthropic’s annual revenue to soar to roughly US$685 billion by that year. To pull off that feat, it will need to fend off AI pricing pressures from cheaper open-weight models, including from Chinese developers.

Anthropic is expected to see a lift from index-tracking funds generating billions of dollars in demand. If it qualifies for early inclusion, it could join the Russell 1000 and the Nasdaq 100 as soon as December. FTSE Russell and Nasdaq changed their rules this year to speed the inclusion of large new listings.

“It popped like any other IPO on the first day but we will need to see solid results in the coming quarters, new use cases for AI, accelerating monetisation, etc, to dispel the gloom in the AI trade,” said Vey-Sern Ling, managing director at Union Bancaire Privee. “Investors don’t have very many fundamental drivers to go on for Anthropic for now. A large part of the value is in the future, which is uncertain, so the share price movements will reflect that.”

title: Saudis strike deal with Japan to replenish depleted oil stocks
article:
(Nov 20): Saudi Arabia reached an agreement to help replenish Japan’s depleted crude stockpiles and expand the kingdom’s own storage capacity in the Asian country.

The accord is further evidence of how major producers and consumers are taking steps to boost energy security after the US-Iran war caused the greatest oil supply disruption in history.

Tokyo will buy as much as eight million barrels of Saudi crude for its national petroleum reserve, subject to favourable market conditions, according to a joint statement on Friday carried by the Saudi Press Agency.

Riyadh will also be given temporary use of 16 million barrels of oil storage capacity in Japan, expanding its existing eight million-barrel holding. The kingdom has already begun to replenish these facilities, according to the statement.

Stockpiles of crude and fuel in consuming nations played a vital role in the initial months of the Middle East war, when tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was almost entirely choked off by Iranian attacks. They helped to ensure sufficient supplies of products like jet fuel through the summer travel season and mitigated price spikes.

Japan released oil from its national reserves last month as part of an effort coordinated by the International Energy Agency (IEA). Overall, IEA members agreed to discharge a record 400 million barrels from emergency stockpiles.

See also: Xi, Trump, Putin agree to increase supply of global fuels

The agreement followed a Nov 9 virtual meeting between Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman and Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Ryosei Akazawa. They reaffirmed the two countries’ strategic partnership and support for long-term energy security, according to the statement.

The recovery in oil flows from Persian Gulf producers to near prewar levels has shifted the conversation in the global market. Brent crude has slumped more than 20% this month to about US$90 a barrel and the world faces a “sizable surplus” next year that’ll drag prices lower, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc.

One of the key questions is how and when major oil importers, which ran down their emergency stockpiles at the height of the Hormuz crisis, will make purchases to rebuild their supply buffers. The Saudi-Japan pact is one of the clearest signs yet that consumers are now considering this.

See also: Oil set for third weekly drop as ample supply outweighs war risk

Major Persian Gulf oil exporters are also looking for ways to increase their resilience in the face of continued threats to shipping through Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has held talks with foreign governments to give state-owned Aramco access to their strategic oil storage. Last month, Singapore agreed to store the kingdom’s oil in caverns from the second half of next year.

The world needs “expanded strategic storage, larger stockpiles of products and flexible refining capacity closer to consumer markets,” Sultan Al Jaber, the chief executive officer of Abu Dhabi National Oil Co, said earlier this month. The company already signed agreements to cooperate on strategic stockpiles with South Korea and India.

title: Malaysia's IOI Properties completes Shenton House acquisition from CEO three years after conflict concerns
article:

The acquisition was completed following payment of a nominal $1 consideration and settlement of $217.06 million in shareholder advances, according to the group's Bursa Malaysia filing.

title: Ubisoft shares plummet after rival games seen hitting sales
article:
(Nov 20): Ubisoft Entertainment SA shares dropped after it forecast a 26% decline in holiday period bookings, when the Assassin’s Creed maker will go up against the new Grand Theft Auto VI in what the French company called a particularly “crowded” season.

Net bookings will fall to about €250 million in the quarter ending in December, it said in a statement on Thursday. That’s down from the €338 million it recorded in the same period a year ago and comes after better-than-expected sales of its newly released Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced game.

The shares dropped 11% to €3.72 at 10.18am in Paris trading on Friday after earlier dropping as much as 15%, the biggest intraday decline since July. The shares have declined 42% this year.

Launched on Thursday from larger rival Take-Two Interactive Software Inc, Grand Theft Auto VI became the best-reviewed video game ever. It’s expected to generate more than US$3 billion of revenue in its first few months and a has had a marketing blitz that dwarfs competing titles.

Ubisoft, which also owns the Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six and Ghost Recon franchises, has struggled with a string of delayed and cancelled games and shrinking orders. Chief executive officer Yves Guillemot has restructured the business into five “creative houses”, including the Vantage Studios business that houses its biggest brands. The company cut 1,100 jobs in the first half of the year.

Bookings in the second quarter were €389 million. That beat analysts’ average forecast €378.6 million according estimates compiled by Bloomberg. The company credited the success of its new Assassin’s Creed title, with more users paying for in-game add ons and premium editions.

See also: Nvidia’s future without founder-CEO Jensen Huang

title: AI’s billions and slick pledges heap pressure on pharma veterans
article:
(Nov 20): As Alphabet Inc’s Isomorphic Labs and Anthropic PBC raise billions and pledge to use artificial intelligence (AI) to cure diseases, traditional pharma companies are feeling the pressure.

Many biotech and pharma executives fretted about tech companies’ speed and intensity, their ability to lure investors with flashy promises, and their potential to go from ally to rival at Europe’s top annual life science event this week. That’s as drugmakers rush to exploit AI themselves.

“It’s a new world for us,” said Charl van Zyl, the chief executive officer of H Lundbeck A/S. The Danish drugmaker has partnerships with AI companies like Cradle Bio BV, notably to boost productivity in research and development, and says it doesn’t see such companies as rivals yet. But “there is always that risk over time that AI companies will become our competitor”.

Isomorphic, which just raised US$5 billion ($6.5 billion) in funding, has partnerships with drugmakers including Novartis AG and Merck & Co — but it’s also developing its own molecules in fields like cancer. CEO Demis Hassabis has said the company would have a drug in trials by the end of this year, which would be faster than traditional pharma timelines.

Anthropic also has six partnerships in drug development as well as its own internal programmes, including in rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, and Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan joined the company’s board this year. Co-founder Dario Amodei predicted in 2024 that AI would help compress the next 50 to 100 years of progress in biology into five to 10 years.

The level of intensity from Big Tech customers like Isomorphic is much higher than had been typical, said Ray Chen, president of GenScript Biotech Corp’s life science unit, which helps companies pair fast lab testing with AI tools. Biology experiments and coding both involve a cycle of “you design, you build, you learn, you do it again”, he said. “But the feedback, the loop, in coding is much faster.”

See also: AI investors have overlooked obvious risks

Some executives said that small and medium-sized drugmakers would likely be able to pivot toward the AI opportunity more quickly than large ones with long-established processes for working in the highly regulated environment of getting drugs approved.

“We’ll never be the frontier tech organisation,” said Sarah Nam, head of AI strategy and partnerships at AbbVie Inc, in a panel at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference. “The best way is really to partner with the right organisations,” she said, and AbbVie is looking for these partners at major AI conferences instead of the usual medical meetings.

See also: Combined wealth of seven co-founders hit US$166 bil after Anthropic IPO

“The most important currency in our business will be speed,” according to Adam Steensberg, the CEO of Zealand Pharma A/S, whose focus is on metabolic diseases like diabetes and obesity. “If you can’t afford speed, it will be a problem.”

Other industry leaders said the question is not just how much faster they can move using AI, but whether the technology can help solve new problems. “AI is about doing things that you couldn’t do before,” said Recursion Pharmaceuticals Inc CEO Najat Khan.

The key is to use the technology as a tool, others said, with success depending on the quality of the data and science underpinning the work.

“The tools we have available today are transformational in terms of how we can think as drug developers,” said Ken Macnamara, CEO of Trogenix, a Scottish startup that uses an AI platform called Odysseus to target cancer cells. Founded in 2023, the company has already begun an early-stage trial in brain tumours. “We couldn’t have brought this medicine to the clinic five years ago.”

Getting an AI-designed medicine into human trials isn’t a computing exercise. It requires work in the lab, tests in animals and design fine-tuning to ensure a potential medicine gets into the body in the most optimal way. Clearing these hurdles may be a challenge for some AI companies.

“Remember a drug is more than ‘do I have a molecule that does something in a person’,” said Alistair Henry, the chief scientific officer at Belgium’s UCB SA.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The proof point of showing that AI-designed drugs can deliver in clinical trials is getting closer, with companies including Generate Biomedicines Inc and Insilico Medicine Cayman TopCo starting late-stage studies. Recursion also agreed on the structure of its late-stage trial with regulators this week.

Another point of concern is where the money is flowing as AI firms grab headlines and attract funding attention.

Belgian biotech Bioxodes, for one, is looking to raise €50 million (US$55 million or $71 million) to fund clinical trials for a stroke treatment derived from tick saliva.

“We definitely see how investors are focusing more on AI,” said CEO Marc Dechamps, “which makes it harder to attract money for biotech companies focused on less hyped areas.”

title: Thailand opens door to US pork, raising risks for farmers
article:
(Nov 20): Thailand crossed a former red line in its trade negotiations with the US, opening its pork market to American competition and adding pressure on a domestic industry already struggling with excess supply and weak prices.

Pork was among the American products granted greater market access as the two countries this week announced agreement on the main terms of a broader trade deal. Thailand also committed to reducing tariffs and other barriers on a range of US goods, though the final agreement has yet to be signed.

The concession highlights the trade-offs Thailand made to keep its exports competitive in the US, its largest overseas market. Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow confirmed to Bloomberg News that pork access was part of the deal, saying after the signing that Bangkok had to make “sacrifices and compromises.”

Pork has long been a protected agricultural market in Thailand. The country had resisted US pressure for greater access for years, including over ractopamine, a growth-promoting feed additive permitted in US production but banned in Thailand.

The Thai Commerce Ministry later on Friday said Thailand won’t open its market to US pork produced using leanness-enhancing agents, following industry concerns and citing risks to public health. At a briefing, Poonpong Naiyanapakorn, the ministry’s permanent secretary, stopped short of answering whether US pork without such additives would be allowed, saying some details of the trade negotiations are confidential.

Thailand is now set to open the sector to competition from one of the world’s biggest pork exporters. For American pork producers, Thailand offers a new but relatively small market. Dan Halstrom, chief executive officer of the US Meat Export Federation, estimates annual sales could reach US$10 million to US$25 million, less than 1% of the value of US pork exports last year.

See also: Asean’s playbook needs to change

Yet the impact on Thailand could be much greater. The country produces enough pork to meet almost all domestic demand, with imports accounting for only about 1% of consumption. Local producers fear even modest volumes of cheaper American meat could further depress prices.

“That may not seem like a large amount, but what we are particularly concerned about is the ability to control the volume,” Anan Traidechapong, a pig farmer and adviser to the Swine Raisers Association of Thailand, said in a phone interview.

The industry was already losing money even before facing new US competition. Thai pig farmers lost a combined 36.7 billion baht from 2023 through 2025, according to the association, which says losses continued this year as production exceeded consumption. Output is forecast to rise to 24.3 million pigs in 2026 from 20.3 million in 2023, with about 95% consumed domestically.

See also: Prabowo said to accept Indonesia vice president resignation

Thai farmers also face a steep price disadvantage, with domestic pork about 35% more expensive than US meat, according to Kasikorn Research Center. It estimates greater US competition could cut the industry’s value by about 112 billion baht, affecting some 149,000 farmers, more than 97% of them smallholders. The number of pig farmers had already fallen by more than a fifth between 2021 and 2024 after years of losses.

Commerce Minister Suphajee Suthumpun said some agricultural products would be subject to safeguards, including import quotas and other controls, to protect domestic producers. She argued that greater market access doesn’t necessarily mean large volumes of American goods will be purchased. “At the end of the day, it’s up to consumers and businesses to decide whether they want to buy,” she said.

The Thai Chamber of Commerce welcomed progress towards a deal that could improve Thai exporters’ access to the US, but chairman Poj Aramwattananont said businesses and farmers exposed to greater foreign competition would need government support.

For pig farmers, the immediate concern is that additional supply could prolong a downturn that has already lasted years. “If this goes ahead,” Anan said, “the industry will never recover”.

title: Singapore’s accountancy sector banked $3.67 bil in 2025 as single accountants cite work as barrier to finding love
article:
Singapore’s accountancy sector enjoyed revenue growth in 2025, recording a 5.1% y-o-y increase in revenue to approximately $3.67 billion, according to the Accounting Entities (AE) Survey 2026 by the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA).

The survey findings were revealed at the annual Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants (ISCA) Conference 2026 on Nov 11. Drawing on responses from 238 AEs, which represented 92% of the sector's estimated revenue, the survey found that sector revenue increased by $177.4 million in 2025.

By service category, business advisory services revenue climbed 12.9% y-o-y to nearly $1.01 billion. This was followed by audit and assurance services, with revenue rising by 3.3% y-o-y to around $1.81 billion, with tax advisory and compliance services revenue climbing 3% y-o-y to around $656.1 million.

The increase in sector revenue is a “positive indicator” of demand for professional services in Singapore, says Shariq Barmaky, country managing partner at Deloitte Singapore. “It shows a continued need for trusted audit, financial reporting and tax work amid an evolving regulatory landscape, and more importantly, a broadening of demand for advice as businesses respond to business transformation, technological change and a more complex operating environment,” he adds.

Overall, average revenue per employee also dipped by 1.2% y-o-y to $147,400. Audit and assurance, the bread and butter of the profession, saw a 3.5% y-o-y drop in this category to approximately $143,400, while rising 4.4% to around $197,900 for business advisory. Corporate support declined 5.4% to roughly $122,600 and tax advisory and compliance dipped slightly (1.7%) to around $207,900.

The survey found that revenue grew across most firm sizes, except micro AEs. The Big 4 AEs, comprising Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC, captured the lion's share (70%) of revenue, bringing in around $2.56 billion, up 4.3% y-o-y.

See also: Hyundai's profit beats estimates on North America, India growth

Meanwhile, large AEs (12 firms), medium AEs (21 firms), small AEs (52 firms) and micro AEs (149 firms) brought in $563 million (up 9.3% y-o-y), $174.2 million (up 12.9% y-o-y), $247 million (up 5.6% y-o-y) and $127.1 million (down 6.2% y-o-y) respectively.

Overseas work was a driver of revenue, with revenue generated from work performed outside Singapore rising by $63.9 million (17.3%) to $432.9 million. Its share of total sector revenue also increased from 11% to 12%, reflecting AEs’ growing international footprint.

Barmaky adds that the higher overseas revenue points to the increasing regional role played by the sector, as businesses look for multidisciplinary advice to navigate complexity and pursue opportunities across markets. “For firms in Singapore, this opens doors to support clients as they grow their business across borders.”

See also: Asian data centre debt binge hitting banks’ limits, Barclays says

Not all segments saw growth, with corporate support revenue declining by 7.4% y-o-y to $192.4 million. Revenue for sustainability-related services also dropped by nearly 27% y-o-y to $24.3 million.

The dip in sustainability-related revenue across the sector may be reflecting a timing shift in line with regulatory milestones, suggests Barmaky.

In August 2025, ACRA and SGX RegCo announced extended timelines for implementing climate reporting requirements, citing the uncertain global economic environment and differences in companies’ resources and reporting readiness. “This may have caused some companies to defer external advisory or sustainability assurance engagements until their obligations become more immediate,” says Barmaky.

He adds that another possible reason for this drop could be due to organisations moving from initial framework design projects to more targeted implementation work. “Early sustainability engagements often involve materiality assessments, establishing emissions baselines, selecting reporting frameworks and setting out policies relating to material ESG factors,” he explains. “Once these foundations are established, subsequent work may be narrower, undertaken internally, or embedded within broader risk, audit, finance transformation or data engagements.”

The AE survey also revealed that Singapore's accountancy workforce grew by 579 positions, or 2.7% y-o-y, from 21,783 in 2024 to 22,362 in 2025. The resident workforce continued to grow, increasing by 522 positions from 16,505 to 17,027 and accounting for 90% of the overall workforce growth.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Workforce expansion was mostly seen in business advisory services and audit and assurance services, with administrative and support functions and tax advisory and compliance services also seeing growth. Not surprisingly, positions of corporate support services decline in line with revenue for the segment.

Accounting for 60% of the workforce, the Big 4 recorded the largest increase in headcount, adding 609 positions in 2025.

According to ACRA, the sector expects to continue expanding its workforce, with AEs reporting more than 1,200 job opportunities available. Around 80% of these opportunities are in audit and assurance and business advisory services.

Median monthly salaries also rose across all surveyed seniority (first-year) levels from 2024 to 2025. Audit assistants saw a 13% y-o-y increase to $3,400; associates earned $4,600, up 10%; senior associates got a 7% pay bump to $5,800; managers received $8,250, or 6% more; and directors’ pay went up 7% to $14,500.

“Our accountancy graduates have high employment rates of more than 93 per cent, and strong median starting salaries,” says Acting Minister for Manpower Jasmin Lau at the ISCA Conference.

The higher salaries reflect employers’ efforts to strengthen their employee value proposition to attract and retain accountancy talent, with the efforts aligned with the recommendations of the Accountancy Workforce Review Committee for firms to review and redesign compensation structures, notes ACRA.

“The survey also showed that median salaries increased across all seniority levels, reflecting that accountancy is an attractive career throughout the career journey of an accountant,” adds Lau.

The AE survey also revealed that wage expenses were 59% of total operating revenue and 70% of total operating expense.

It is an open secret that Singaporean workers clock long hours at work, which makes it challenging to balance career with other responsibilities. The country also suffers from an ageing population, with the country’s total fertility rate hitting a new low of 0.87 in 2025.

As Singapore has started reviewing how it can better support marriage and parenthood, ISCA, the national accountancy body, initiated a survey of its members to get their perspectives on the matter to ensure that they were represented in this national conversation. A snippet report, entitled Marriage and parenthood among early and mid-career accountancy professionals, was released on Nov 11. The survey managed to gather responses from 585 individuals aged 21 to 45 years-old. This age group represented 54% of ISCA’s membership base.

The survey also included a focus group discussion with ISCA’s Young Professionals Advisory Committee. ISCA adds that the survey findings should not be interpreted as statistically representative of all accountancy professionals in Singapore.

Unsurprisingly, the survey reveals that work demands reduce the time, energy and opportunities available to form meaningful relationships for single accountancy professionals. 79% of singles say that work reduces relationship opportunities, with 64% of singles indicating they were open to marriage or intending to marry.

On challenges to finding a partner, out of a sample size of 138, social fatigue after work was cited by 63.8% as a barrier to relationship forming. Other barriers, each cited by more than 40% of this sample, include long working hours, difficulty in finding a compatible partner and limited social circles.

Meanwhile, 81% of all respondents feel pressure to be visible to demonstrate their commitment to work, while close to 70% were concerned that taking time away for parenting or caregiving could affect their career progression. 57% of respondents believe that they have experienced or observed caregiving-related career disadvantage, while only only 35% felt they could use flexible work arrangements without facing negative judgement or scrutiny.

Recognising changing career needs from its survey, ISCA is piloting FlexConnect, a flexible hiring initiative that connects experienced accountancy professionals seeking alternative work arrangements with businesses that need finance talent for specific periods or assignments.

The initiative offers employers access to professionals for contract, fractional and temporary roles, including support for project needs, peak workloads and employees taking extended leave.

Since the pilot began in September 2026, more than 100 accountancy professionals have registered their interest to explore flexible work opportunities, while receiving support from employers across industries, including public and private sector organisations, shares ISCA.

ISCA President Lee Boon Teck stresses that a strong profession “should offer more than one way” to build a successful career. He says: “As professionals move through different stages of life, their interests and priorities may change, but the experience and expertise they have developed remain valuable. At the same time, businesses need greater flexibility in how they access talent, whether to support a specific project, manage peak workloads or cover temporary staffing gaps.

“Through ISCA FlexConnect, we hope to bring these needs together and create more opportunities for professionals to remain engaged in the workforce. Our ambition is to make accountancy a profession where people can continue to grow and contribute throughout their careers.”

title: Lufthansa to eliminate 1,000 jobs at struggling flagship airline
article:
(Nov 20): Deutsche Lufthansa AG will cut 1,000 jobs at its namesake airline to turn around the unprofitable mainline unit, as high fuel costs put more pressure on Europe’s largest aviation group.

The company will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees seen by Bloomberg. Lufthansa Airlines also plans to further reduce capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and shrink its fleet of Airbus A320 aircraft, switching to the smaller A220 type, it said.

The planned reductions are the second culling in little over a year and reveal the extent of the struggles to revive the fortunes of the airline’s flagship product. The airline group announced last September that it intended to cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030.

Lufthansa is undergoing its biggest efficiency drive in years as high jet-fuel prices and an underperforming mainline airline weigh on results. Lufthansa Airlines posted an operating loss of €180 million ($232 million) in the first nine months.

“After two years of the turnaround, we have to acknowledge that the original measures are no longer sufficient to secure our future,” management wrote in the letter. “In fact, 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, persistently high fuel costs, nine days of strikes and our already very high cost base have made the situation more acute.”

Lufthansa’s new supervisory board chairman, Johannes Teyssen, said earlier this year that “significantly greater efforts” may be needed to improve the airline’s flagging performance after losing ground to rivals in what he called self-inflicted damage.

See also: US flight chaos persists with thousands of cancellations, delays

The measures revealed on Friday come as Lufthansa tries to resolve a dispute with labour unions, though no agreement had been reached so far.
